1:
Who is speaking is settled before anything else. Gill identifies the voice as Jehovah the Son of God, the eternal Word, very probably appearing in a human form, since there was an object seen as well as a voice heard. Henry says the same and draws the parallel out: not a created angel but the second person of the Trinity, by whom the worlds were made, and the same who afterwards spoke from Sinai, beginning here with the creation of the world and there with the redemption of Israel out of Egypt, from both of which the necessity of our subjection is inferred. Wesley agrees and describes the setting, a dark and thick cloud out of which a tempestuous wind was sent as the harbinger of the presence. Gill adds that Elihu had seen the storm rising and hastened to finish, and that it was raised to give notice of the appearing and to command reverence and attention; the Targum, he notes, calls it the whirlwind of distress, which answers to the condition Job was in. Clarke works on the Hebrew and finds a different word from the one used a chapter earlier, meaning something turbulent and violently agitated, what we should call a tempest, and intended to fill Job's mind with an awful sense of the divine majesty; he reports that the Chaldee renders it a whirlwind of grief, which makes the scene allegorical rather than real and sets it in Job's imagination.

Why the answer comes now rather than earlier is Henry's contribution. When they had all had their saying and yet had not gained their point, it was time for God to interpose, whose judgement is according to truth. Job had silenced his three friends without convincing them of his integrity; Elihu had silenced Job without bringing him to acknowledge his mismanagement of the dispute; and God now does both, convincing Job of his unadvised speaking and then putting honour on him by convincing the three that they had wronged him. Ellicott reads the same moment as the structural climax of the poem, since nothing could remain but darkness unless he whose government was the matter in dispute intervened; and he states the single argument that the remaining chapters develop, that there is so much in nature which man neither knows nor can understand that it is absurd for him to suppose he can judge aright in matters touching God's moral government. He notes too that although Job is justified later, the tone of everything said to him here is more or less mingled with reproach.
2:
The opening question is read as a rebuke rather than an inquiry. Gill denies it is addressed to Elihu, as some have thought, since it was Job the Lord answered and Job who took the words to himself, and explains that God asks not as ignorant but as wondering that such a man should talk so. Keil and Delitzsch argue from the participle that Job must have uttered such words immediately before and been interrupted by Jehovah without any intervening speaker, and notice that the word for counsel deliberately stands without the possessive. Clarke paraphrases it as a challenge to one who pretends to speak on the deep things of God and leaves his counsels the darker for the explanation. Ellicott answers the question from Job's own earlier words, that this is a dying and enfeebled man, not even a man in his best estate but one persecuted and exhausted, and therefore altogether unequal to the task he has undertaken. Wesley marks the effect rather than the sense, that this first word struck Job to the heart and is echoed back by him at the end as the arrow that stuck fast in him.

The summons that follows is military. Gill has Job girded like a man of valour putting on his harness for battle, the allusion being to the long eastern garments that had to be gathered up for work or war, and observes that Job had blustered what he would do and is now dared to do it. Clarke hears reassurance in it as well as challenge, since the questions to come are easier than those Job had presumed to discuss, and he notes that the most convincing manner of arguing is by interrogation, the form in which the best orations of the ancients were cast.

Gregory stands back from the rebuke to ask why it was needed at all. After the loss of his goods, the death of his children, the wounds of his body, his wife's persuasion to evil and the insulting language of his comforters, Job ought to have been praised by his Judge for such constancy, had he been about to be called out of this present world. But since he is to receive back twofold and be restored to his former health, Almighty God is obliged in strict justice to reprove the man he preserves alive, lest his very victory lay him low with the sword of pride; for nothing commonly slays a soul more fatally than the consciousness of virtue, which puffs it up with self-consideration, deprives it of the fulness of truth, and by suggesting that it is sufficient of itself for the attainment of rewards diverts it from the intention of improvement. Job was just before his scourges, Gregory concludes, and remained more just after them, raised the higher in the praise of God as he was smitten with the heavier chastisement.
4:
The first question is about presence, and every witness takes it as a measure of the distance between the two speakers. Clarke paraphrases it bluntly, that Job has a limited and derived being and is only of yesterday, so what can he know, and Wesley puts the same in a sentence, that one who is but of yesterday presumes to judge eternal counsels. Henry turns it into a pair of propositions, the greatness of God who laid the foundations and the meanness of a man not so much as present, and observes that we had no hand in the making of the world and so nothing in it entitles us to a dominion over it. Gill sharpens it by putting Job in a state of nothingness, a mere nonentity when the work was done, who yet takes upon himself to dive into the secret ways of Providence. He also notes the oddity in the figure: the earth has foundations so firm that it cannot be moved, yet what can they be, since it hangs in the air upon nothing, and can be no other than the power and will of God. Ellicott reads the architectural comparison as a concession to the feebleness of man, one that itself heightens the effect of the answer the question compels.

The builder's tools in the next verses are taken literally by some and pressed into astronomy by others. Wesley keeps to the plain sense, the measuring line that regulates the dimensions and the corner stone in which the stability of a building consists. Gill says God laid the measures out in his divine mind and forth by his divine power, and then turns the question on the learned: mathematicians pretend to give us the circumference and diameter of the earth but are not agreed and widely differ, which shows they are at no certainty; he adds that the clause may be rendered so as to read a severe sarcasm, since such a knowing man as Job must needs know this. Clarke reaches for the physics, asking who adjusted the polar and equatorial distances from the centre, who formed the zones and great circles, and who fitted the magnitude and gravity of the whole to its orbit, concluding that the questions show an unfathomable depth of counsel. Gill reports two Jewish readings of the sockets the foundations are sunk in, pillars or the mountains, and answers that nothing visible supports a world that hangs on nothing.

What sang at the founding is the one point genuinely in dispute. Clarke holds that the words must refer to intelligent beings existing before the visible heavens, and takes both clauses for the angelic host, first though perhaps not chief in the order of creation, whose own making may be included in the word heavens at the opening of Genesis; the Chaldee renders it all the troops of angels, and these witnessed the work and celebrated it when it was finished. Ellicott agrees that the context suggests the angels entrusted with the guardianship of the stars, and remarks that Milton borrowed his conceptions from this and that the sublimity of the expression needs no comment. Wesley explains both titles, morning stars for their lustre and sons of God because they had their whole being from him and were partakers of his image, and draws the inference Job is meant to feel, that they neither advised nor assisted in the work, nor censured any part of it, as Job had presumed to do. Gill alone keeps the literal sense open, since though strictly there is but one morning star all may be so called, being created early in the world's morning and shining brightest nearest the dawn; and he adds the figurative readings, angels for their purity and number, ministers as the stars in Christ's right hand, and Christ himself as the principal morning star.
8:
The sea is introduced as a newborn child, and the commentators follow the figure clause by clause. Gill marks the transition as following the order of creation, from the earth to the sea, and insists the verses describe not the flood, as some interpret them, but the first creation, the sea being represented throughout as an infant, here still in embryo and shut up in the bowels of the earth as a child in its mother's womb, that hollow being the storehouse where God first laid up the deep waters. Clarke calls it a very fine metaphor, the sea issuing from the womb of the void and formless chaos, and finds even the delicate circumstance that precedes a birth alluded to. Wesley states the plain question under the image, who it was that set bounds to the vast and raging ocean and shut it up as with doors in its proper place, so that it might not overflow the earth.

The clothing of the child is read the same way, and Clarke presses the detail hardest. The cloud answers to the cloth in which a new-born infant is first received, and the thick darkness to the swathing that supports a body too tender to bear even careful handling; the image, he says, quoting another writer, is exquisitely maintained, since the young ocean issues from the womb of chaos and is dressed as an infant would be. He adds an allusion to the opening of Genesis, where darkness is said to be on the face of the deep, which here becomes the swaddling band of the new-born sea. Wesley takes the vapours and clouds that rise from the sea and hover over it as the garment, and the black clouds as the bands that keep it within its bounds, but then withdraws the figure to make the point it was for: neither clouds, nor air, nor sands, nor shores can bound the sea, but God alone. Keil and Delitzsch set the scene in the order of the primeval states, the formless void being the first half and the deep the second half of the earth's early condition, and note that the question passes over the intermediate stage in which the waters of the sky and of the earth were not yet separated.
10:
The cradle prepared for the child is described as an act of violence to the earth. Gill renders the clause with an older English translator as breaking the earth by decree, a vast chasm made to hold the waters, God cleaving the ground, raising the hills and sinking the valleys so that channels were formed to carry the waters to their appointed place; this he refers to the work of the second day. Wesley describes the same hollow places as a cradle to receive and hold so great and goodly an infant, with bounds fixed as strongly as if fortified with bars and doors. Clarke traces the decree to the command in Genesis that the waters under the heavens be gathered into one place and the dry land appear, and identifies the bars and doors with the geography itself, the dry land everywhere forming a barrier against the encroachments of the sea, and the great rivers, bays and creeks the doors by which it passes into the interior of continents. Ellicott prefers a different rendering, that God prescribed for it his decree rather than broke up a place, and adds the reflection the verse invites: bearing in mind the vast forces and unstable nature of the sea, it seems a marvel that it acknowledges any limits at all.

On the word that halts the waves the two who comment part company in method. Gill keeps to the coasts and the tides, the sea spreading to such and such shores and no further, its rolling tides running up the rivers that go out of it and returning, keeping exactly to time and place because the Word of God has said so, and obeying through his almighty power. Clarke answers the same question mechanically and at length, tracing the limitation of the tides to the attraction of the sun and moon, to the gravitation of the earth's own parts toward its centre, and above all to the rotation which carries any point of the surface out from under the direct attractive influence before the waters can be raised to any extraordinary height; these, he concludes, are among the bars and doors by which the proud waves are stayed, and a world of wisdom and management was necessary to settle them.
12:
The question about the morning is heard as a question about authority over a thing nobody controls. Gill observes that Job had lived to see many a morning but it never was in his power to command one, and had sometimes wished for the light before its time without being able to hasten it. Wesley reads the challenge as covering the whole order, whether Job created the sun and appointed the succession of day and night, and notes that the work was done long before he was born. Henry makes the light the first of six things Job is challenged to account for, and turns its very familiarity into the argument: there is no visible being of which we are more firmly assured, and none we are more puzzled to describe; we welcome the day-spring, but it was not commanded since our days, it knew its place before we knew ours, for we are but of yesterday, and the constant succession of day and night was no contrivance of ours but shows the glory of God.

The second clause about the dayspring knowing its place is where the astronomy enters. Ellicott glosses it briefly, that the place changes from day to day with the changing seasons, and Wesley says the same, that the point of the heavens where it should arise varies every day. Clarke takes the whole matter much further. The first clause he refers to the dawn, the twilight produced by the refraction of the solar rays in the atmosphere, by which the light reaches us gradually instead of bursting at once upon eyes it would otherwise injure, and by which the sun's body becomes visible some minutes before it rises above the horizon. The second he refers to the annual revolution, since the earth's course through the ecliptic carries it north and south of the equinoctial so that the sun appears to change his place each day, and the dawn does not appear nor the sun rise in exactly the same point of the horizon on two successive days in the whole year; and from this declination north and south follow both the points of rising and setting and the length of day and night.

What the morning does when it comes is read morally. Gill has the light take hold of the extremities of the hemisphere as soon as it springs, and applies the image to the spread of the Gospel to the ends of the earth. Wesley describes the same instant spreading from one end of the hemisphere to the other, and explains the effect on the wicked by two causes, that the light discovers them where darkness hid them, and that morning was the usual time for executing judgment. Clarke makes the picture concrete: as soon as the light dawns the thieves, assassins and adulterers who hate and shun it fly like ferocious beasts to their dens and hiding places. He also proposes a rearrangement of the text, holding that the verse about the light withheld from the wicked connects immediately with this one and that the verse about the seal disturbs the connection; and he explains the withholding as their own preference, since men who prowl after their prey at night must sleep by day. Ellicott identifies the figure precisely as that of a man shaking out a cloth.
14:
The image of the seal is explained two ways. Gill, Wesley and Ellicott all take the clay for the earth itself, shapeless in the dark, a mere waste and void like the chaos at the beginning, and receiving a form under the light as clay receives the impress of a seal, so that the rising hills and spreading dales stand forth as in their proper raiment. Wesley distinguishes what it is that stands forth, the natural things such as living creatures, herbs and trees, and the artificial, such as houses and other buildings. Clarke reads the clay as the earth's capacity to modify itself into endless forms, and points to the variety of plants and flowers and fruits as the proof, adding an antiquarian note on the Eastern brass seals for stamping pottery, six of which lay on his own desk with fine clay still in their perforations; the garment on this reading is the decoration of the surface by what springs from it under solar light and heat. He reports besides another translator who applies the whole verse to the rays of light rather than to the ground. Gill adds the spiritual application he finds throughout the passage, the change the light of the Gospel makes in men.

The last clause of the section is taken up separately. Gill explains the light withheld from the wicked as the loss of what they counted light, since their day is the night and it is taken from them when the morning breaks, and he allows two figurative senses besides, the light of prosperity removed and the light of life extinguished when they are sent into outer darkness. Wesley divides the withholding between two causes, their own choice, since they prefer darkness to light, and the judgement of God or of the magistrate, by which they are cut off from the light of the living; and he glosses the broken arm as the great strength they had used in oppressing others. Clarke reports a rendering that turns the clause differently again, so that what is broken off is the roving of wickedness, the wicked being no longer able to pursue their predatory excursions.
16:
What the springs of the sea are is disputed before anything is said about entering them. Gill offers a range of renderings: the subterranean passages through which waters flow into the sea, or the fountains rising at its bottom, of which some report springs of fresh water even where the deep water is saltier than the surface; or the drops of the sea, which no one can consider and count; or, with one of the Targums, its perplexities, its thickets, of which some speak as woods and forests; or its rocks and shelves; or its borders, so that the question becomes whether Job has travelled the whole ocean to its utmost edge. Wesley keeps to the Hebrew figure, that the word is tears, the springs out of which the waters flow as tears do from the eyes. Ellicott prefers the mazes and intricacies of a trackless and pathless deep, and notes that this leads on naturally to the cognate thought of the bottomless pit of death in the next verse. Clarke admits the limit plainly: of these springs, inlets or outlets we know just as much as Job did, and he reports the opinion once prevalent among philosophers that fresh matter constantly oozed in through a porous bottom to supply the sea, with the obvious objection that through such pores the materials might as well ooze out as in. Of the second clause he says only that no man since Job has found the depths out, and that in multitudes of places they remain unfathomed.

The gates of death are treated as the strongest case of the argument from ignorance. Gill specifies which gates are meant, not the causes by which death entered the world but those by which men pass into the state of the dead, and lists what is hidden: we do not know experimentally what death is, nor in what way or at what time or in what place we shall go out of the world, nor what the state of the dead is, since there is no correspondence between them and the living, and the gates of those dark and invisible regions have never been thrown open for mortals to look in. Wesley says the same at more length and with more feeling, that death is a grand secret, that we cannot describe how the knot is untied between soul and body, and that while we are here in a world of sense we speak of the world of spirits as blind men do of colours, and shall be amazed on arriving to find how much we were mistaken. Clarke fastens on the two terms the verse distinguishes, death and the shadow of death, taking the second for the intermediate state, the openings into the place of separate spirits, and presses a logical difficulty: it will not do to call death the privation of life, for what then would the shadow of that privation be?

The breadth of the earth closes the series with a question of measurement. Gill takes the word for all the dimensions but especially the surface, and answers that a man who lived as long as Methuselah and spent every day at it could never survey all the hills and dales, rocks and mountains, cities and towns and forests and rivers, some parts being inaccessible to the most skilful geometer. Clarke and Ellicott both note that the language belongs to an older picture of the world, in which the earth was a vast extended plain bordered by the ocean and the sky, its circumference unknown; and Ellicott adds the observation that although all this language is unscientific, its majestic sublimity is not one whit affected thereby.
19:
The question where light dwells is heard by two witnesses as a question about the nature of light itself. Gill glosses it narrowly as the way to the place where light dwells and what that place is. Clarke turns it into a challenge to natural philosophy: what is the source of light, and indeed what is light? It is not in the sun, for light was before the sun; it is doubtless a substance, but of what kind, and of what particles? And as for darkness, is it philosophical to call it the mere privation of light? He will think philosophy has made some advance toward accuracy, he says, when it can tell us what cold is and what darkness is, leaving mere privations out of the question. Wesley asks the same in the older idiom, where the sun goes when it departs from this hemisphere and where the tabernacle is in which he is supposed to rest; and since there was a time when nothing but gross darkness was upon the face of the earth, by what way did light come into the world, and whence was the orderly succession of light and darkness fetched? Was this thy work, he ends, or wast thou privy to it, a counsellor or an assistant in it?

The next verse imagines Job conducting them home, and the commentators differ on how literally to take the picture. Gill applies it chiefly to the light, taken as it were by the hand and guided to its utmost bound, and answers that only the Lord does this, having set a tabernacle for the sun which goes forth at his command as a strong man to run a race, never missing its way or erring from its path. Wesley reads the bound as the whole course from the place of abode whence the light is supposed to come to the end of its journey. Ellicott glosses the verb simply as going with or tracking it. Clarke observes that darkness and light are here personified, each as a real intelligent being with a separate existence and a local dwelling, and defends the liberty: poetry animates everything, being the region of fictitious existence.

The closing verse is where the tone of the whole passage becomes unmistakable. Clarke calls it another strong and biting irony and argues that a literal rendering proves it, since the words say outright that Job knows because he was born then and the number of his days is great. Ellicott agrees and draws the practical conclusion for translators, that the verse is better read without an interrogation as sublime irony. Gill alone answers it as a plain question, replying that Job was not born when light and darkness were first separated and had their several apartments assigned them and their bounds set, and adding that even the first man could not have been present, since man was not made until the sixth day. Clarke states plainly what he takes the irony to be for: Job had valued himself too much on his knowledge, and a chief object of this august speech is to humble that knowing pride and send him to seek true wisdom and humility where they are to be found.
22:
The treasuries of snow and hail are explained first as a figure and then as a physical question. Gill identifies them with the vapours raised and the clouds formed in the atmosphere, which is the storehouse of those meteors, and gives three reasons for the word treasure: they are hidden until they fall, they are in the keeping and at the command of their proprietor, and they are enriching, since snow lying on the earth keeps it warm and makes it fruitful. He then guards the image against being pressed, warning that we are not to imagine heaps laid up in times past against times to come, but that God can produce them when he pleases as easily as a man with a full store can bring his goods out at once. Wesley keeps the plain question, whether Job knows where those vast quantities are laid up which God draws forth when he sees fit. Clarke prefers to ask how they are made, allowing that snow is easier to account for than hail. Hail is commonly supposed to be raindrops frozen in passing through cold regions of the air, and its size proportioned to the drop it came from, yet it is plainly not formed from a single drop, being composed of many small spherules frozen together, sometimes soft at the centre and sometimes built on a hard nucleus; he prefers the account which traces both snow and hail to electricity, the hail forming in the higher and colder regions where the electric matter is abundant and gathering further particles as it falls, and he admits candidly that this theory is not in all cases supported by the facts.

What the store is kept for is read by everyone as judgement. Gill takes the time of trouble for the punishment or affliction of men and lets the next clause explain it. Clarke offers a different sense for the first phrase, the season of strictness, when the earth is bound by the frost, and then points to the history behind the second, since hailstones have often been the instruments of God's displeasure; he finds probable allusions both to the plague of hail on Egypt and to the destructive shower that fell on the Canaanitish kings who fought against Israel. Ellicott names the same battle in a single line.

The parting of the light divides the commentators more sharply than anything else in the chapter. Gill takes it of daylight and offers several possibilities: the first division of light from darkness, or the daily separation at sunrise and sunset, or the two hemispheres where darkness lies on one and light on the other, or the poles with their six months of each by turns, or the unequal distribution of day and night in different seasons and climates, or that particular day when there was darkness over all Egypt and light in Goshen. He notes that some understand the verse of lightning and objects that lightning is mentioned later. Wesley reads it as Gill does, of light variously distributed in the world, shining in one place and time when it does not shine in another, and explains the second clause by the old notion that the sun is the father of the winds, drawing up the exhalations that give them matter, the east wind in particular being often observed to rise with the sun. Clarke takes the verse of lightning after all, and turns it into a catalogue of what electrical science had not settled: whether it is a simple element or a compound, what its velocity is, why it is not conducted by every kind of substance although it exists in all, how its particles cohere and in what order they are propagated, and above all how the zigzag form is produced, which he calls the curious and indescribable parting the verse asks about.
25:
Where the watercourse runs is settled before anything else, and the answer is that it runs in the air. Gill rules out an aqueduct or canal of the kind men cut from the Nile to flood their fields, and puts the channel in the atmosphere, a course for the rain to come down by, steered so that it falls regularly and gently rather than in spouts and floods, in drops larger or smaller and on whatever part of the earth God pleases; and he adds a Jewish commentator's refinement, that every drop has its own canal. Wesley says the same more briefly, that without this providence the showers would fall confusedly and overwhelm the earth. Ellicott corrects the rendering to a channel cleft for the water-flood. Clarke goes the other way and derives the word from a root meaning to ascend, so that the term may mean a cloud, where the waters are stored, since he cannot see how a torrent can be said to ascend except by evaporation; by that contrivance, he notes, the earth is not only watered but dried, so that too much moisture is not left lying on the ground, which would destroy what it was meant to nourish. He wonders whether a waterspout might be intended.

The path made for the thunderbolt is where Clarke and Henry make their largest claims. Clarke renders it a path for the bolt of thunder, has God launching it and making the road it runs in, and observes that heathenism reserved the grasping and darting of the thunderbolt to its supreme god, none of the inferior deities being capable of it. Wesley asks who opened a passage for the lightning and thunder out of the cloud in which they were imprisoned, and notes that they are joined with the rain here because they commonly accompany great showers. Henry turns the whole group of verses into the second half of the argument: hitherto the questions have been fitted to convince Job of his ignorance, and now, in the same manner, they are to show his impotence, since it is as little that he can do as that he knows, and he should therefore no more oppose the proceedings of Providence than arraign its counsels. Wesley marks the same turn in a sentence. Henry adds that nothing is more uncertain than what weather it shall be, or further out of our reach to appoint, and that God divides the water-course so exactly that the rain is directed where to fall even when the shower is most violent, with as much certainty as if it ran in conduit-pipes.

That the rain falls where nobody lives is the point the passage has been driving at. Gill notes that the wilderness is uninhabited because it is dry and barren, that there is no one there to cultivate or water it as a garden is watered and no one to profit by the rain, and yet the Lord sends it for the use of the animals that dwell there, which shows his providence extending even to the wild beasts; and he reads the desolate ground, so thirsty that it is among the things which never say it is enough, as an emblem of the Gentile world satisfied at last by the rain of the Gospel. Ellicott puts the same conclusion in a line, that God is mindful of his creation independently of the wants of man. Clarke reaches it from the meteorology he has been expounding: the thunder cloud is conducted over deserts as well as over inhabited countries, and this to make the tender herb spring, since the beasts and fowls and insects that inhabit the wilderness must be nourished by what the ground produces, every tribe of animals having been made by the hand of God and even the lowest of them supported by his providence.
28:
The question about parentage is the shortest in the chapter and the commentators answer it flatly. Gill says the rain has no father but God, and notes that even the heathens gave their supreme god a title of that kind; whatever secondary causes there may be, God only is the efficient cause and producer, and Gill takes the same for a figure of the Gospel, which is not of men but comes down from heaven and tarries not for man. Wesley reduces it to a single line, whether any man can beget or produce rain at his pleasure. Clarke turns instead to the dew, renders the second word as the small round globules, and quotes a definition of dew as a thin insensible mist descending slowly while the sun is below the horizon, differing from rain as less from more. He then reports an unsettled controversy, since experiments had been made to determine whether dew rises from the earth or descends from the atmosphere and had alternately favoured each; the question, he concludes, is not yet decided, so that we can no more tell than Job which has begotten the drops of dew, and he asks whether it may simply be water deposited from the air when the ground is colder than the air above it. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the parallelism asks after a begetter in the one line and a bearer in the other, and that rain and dew have no created father as ice and hoar-frost have no created mother.

The freezing of water is where Clarke stops to expound the physics. Gill keeps to the figure and calls God the parent of ice as of rain and dew, noting that Scripture elsewhere calls it his ice, his own offspring, and that the verse represents the Lord as a mother, a way of speaking he finds in an ancient poet who joined both parents in one name. Clarke defines ice as a solid, transparent and brittle body formed of water by cold, and lays out the theory current in his day that ice is really the natural state of water, its fluidity being a kind of fusion like that of metals, differing only in how much fire is required; on that view water is solid by nature and made fluid by heat. He explains why ice floats by the air-bubbles produced in freezing, which make it lighter than water in the proportion of eight to nine, and notes their expansive power, sufficient to burst the strongest containing vessel.

The last verse of the group is read literally by two and figuratively by a third. Ellicott renders it that the waters hide themselves and become like stone, losing their familiar quality altogether. Clarke takes the reference to be to winter freezing, confirmed by the constellations named just afterwards, which rise in the winter months, and observes that the surface is sometimes as hard as stone and that even the seas are locked up from all purposes of navigation for months together, not only within the polar circles but in Norway and Sweden and Denmark and Holland and parts of Germany. Gill describes the same hardening, a surface that will bear great burdens and let carriages pass where ships went before, and then turns it into an emblem of the hard heart of man, which only the power and grace of God can thaw.
31:
The two constellations are read as the two seasons, and the question as one about the calendar. Wesley states it most plainly: the seven stars bring in the spring and the other constellation rises in November and brings in winter, so that both summer and winter will have their course; God can change them when he pleases, making the spring cold and the winter warm, and so binding the one and loosing the other, but we cannot. Clarke gives the astronomy, six stars of the cluster visible to the naked eye and seven to a good eye on a clear night, though a telescope will show ten times that number; and he passes on another writer's judgement that the winter constellation stands by a correct and elegant figure for winter at large, the two being opposed as the vernal renovation of nature is opposed to its wintry destruction. He adds a caution of his own about all these identifications, that he finds them certain where he is obliged to doubt, and is reluctant to depart from the ancient versions but dares not follow where he cannot see the groundwork. Gill takes the first phrase as the pleasantnesses of the season, which cannot be hindered from taking place in the proper course of the year, and reports the alternative rendering, the bands of the cluster, on which the question becomes whether Job could gather and bind such a group together; he applies the whole to the irresistible influences of grace, which make a springtime in souls where it was before winter. Ellicott weighs the same two senses, influence or band, and thinks the parallel with the bands of the other constellation favours the second.

The names in the next verse are less certain still. Gill identifies the first with the chambers of the south, the southern pole and its stars, hidden from sight in this part of the globe and named from a root meaning to separate, while noting that some take it for the twelve signs of the zodiac. Ellicott takes the zodiac reading as the common one and identifies the children of the northern constellation with the three stars in the tail of the Bear. Wesley divides the verse between the southern signs and the northern, and glosses the sons as the lesser stars placed round about the greater and attending on them as children on their parents. Clarke reports a quite different derivation, from a root meaning to corrupt, on which the word would name the pestilential summer wind of Arabia rather than any constellation at all.

The closing question about the ordinances of heaven is taken by everyone as the summary of the section. Gill describes them as laws settled by the decree and will of God concerning the situation, motion, operation and influence of the stars, constantly observed and so far from being made by men that they are not even fully known by them. Wesley puts the two halves of the question separately, whether Job gave these laws or perfectly knows them, and whether he can manage and overrule their influences. Clarke asks whether Job is a thorough astronomer and then turns the question on his own century: Newton has given much light, and his system is most probably the true one, but gravity is essential to it and Newton could neither explain nor comprehend what gravity is, nor are his followers one whit wiser; no man has yet fully found out the ordinances of heaven or their dominion on the earth.
34:
The two questions about commanding the weather are read as a contrast of voices. Clarke puts it exactly: thunder is called voices in the Hebrew because it is reckoned the voice of God, so that Job's voice is here set against the voice of Jehovah, and the question is whether he can produce the lightning and thunder by which the water is formed and poured down. Gill draws the practical distinction the verse implies. Job may call to the clouds as long as he likes and not a drop will be let down, because rain is not to be had in a dictatorial and authoritative way but in a suppliant one, through the prayer of faith, as Elijah had it; the clouds are at the disposal of the Lord, and are to be asked for and not commanded.

The lightnings reporting for orders draw the same answer at greater length. Gill imagines the errand completed and the messengers returned to wait for further orders, and then presses what it would mean if such a power lay with men: Elijah indeed called down fire on the captains and their fifties, but under the impulse of the spirit of prophecy and not for imitation, and when the disciples wanted the same on a provocation they were severely reproved; were lightnings at the call of men, dreadful things would be done in the world, for if good men when provoked would use such a power to destroy life, how much more bad men. Clarke notes that the heathen made their chief god the holder of the forked lightning, grasping the bickering flame so that it cannot escape however it struggles, and he remarks on the Hebrew word for lightnings, which carries both the sense and the sound of thunder.

The verse about wisdom in the inward parts is admitted on all hands to be difficult. Gill takes it of man and reads it as continuing the argument, that no such wisdom has been put in him as would guide the stars or direct the clouds and the lightning. Ellicott confesses that the mention of the inward parts and the heart in the middle of natural phenomena perplexes everyone, and proposes the natural solution of referring them to the lightnings just personified, so that the question asks who put such understanding into them. Clarke keeps the human sense and turns it into a reflection on the limits of thought, that the most sedulous attention and the deepest contemplation cannot investigate truth without the inspiration of the Almighty, and that a man who knows nothing of his own mind or the mode of its operations can hardly comprehend the Spirit which is infinite; but he reports the alternative that refers the whole verse to the lightnings, and notices how widely the old versions diverge here, one of them reading the clause of women and embroidery and another of the cock.
37: The closing pair of questions returns to the clouds and the ground. Gill allows two senses for numbering the clouds, counting them when the heavens are full or declaring their matter and motion and use, neither of which any man can do completely, and reports a Jewish reading on which the question is who can make the sky clear as sapphire when it is overcast; he notes too that clouds are used elsewhere to denote a great multitude, since nobody has wisdom enough to count them when the heavens are full of them. Clarke suggests that the verb may bear an Arabic sense and mean to irradiate, referring to the inimitable tinges sometimes seen in the sky, and explains the bottles of heaven as an allusion to the skin bottles in which water was carried from wells and tanks. Ellicott notes that the second clause is understood in two opposite senses, of pouring the bottles out or of laying them up in store, and that the choice is hard because the following clause is itself uncertain, according as the hardened ground is taken for thick mud or for dry soil; with this verse, he observes, the survey of physical phenomena ends. Clarke reads the hardening as a question about the cohesion of matter itself and answers it with a chemist's catalogue, asking how measured parts of alumine and silex and oxide of iron make a ruby, or silex and water an opal, and how such worthless dusts grow into hardness and form an emerald. Gill reads the hardened ground the other way, as dust attenuated and ground into powder while the clods cleave together as if glued, which happens in a drought for want of rain, though he allows the opposite case of the bottles of heaven being unstopped and poured out. Clarke presses his question further than mineralogy usually goes, asking what the principle of cohesion among the particles of matter can be, and noting that even water in a solid form enters into several gems as their water of crystallization; how such solids and fluids of differing natures grow into hardness and form one curious mineral is a question he does not think anyone can solve.
39:
The turn from weather to animals is noticed by everyone. Gill marks it plainly, that from meteors the Lord passes to beasts and birds, and reports that some begin the next chapter here since it treats of nothing else; Clarke says the same more firmly, that the best Hebrew Bibles begin the new chapter with this verse and begin it properly, the preceding one having belonged to astronomy and meteorology and this opening the natural history of the animal kingdom. Ellicott agrees in a line. Wesley states the question the turn carries, whether it is by Job's care that lions living in desert places are furnished with their necessary provisions.

The lion is chosen as the hardest case. Gill calls him the strongest and fiercest of beasts and answers that man neither can hunt for him nor would dare to if he could, whereas the Lord does; and he passes on two things reported by the naturalists, that a small creature between a fox and a wolf goes before the lion and hunts the prey for him, and that young lions hunt for the old ones when these are no longer able to go in search themselves, bringing the prey back or calling them to share it. Clarke prefers to render the word of the lioness and turns the question on Job's own equipment: has he the animal's instinct, does he know the habits and haunts of the creatures it hunts, when he has neither its strength nor its instinct nor its cunning?

The couching in the dens is explained two ways. Clarke refers it to the young, before they are capable of trusting themselves abroad or fleet enough to run their prey down, so that they lie under cover to surprise what they could not overtake; and he derives the Hebrew name for a lion's whelp from a root meaning to cover or hide, which fits that habit exactly. Gill reports the reading that makes them old lions lying couchant for want of strength and waiting for whatever passes, but objects that the same coverts serve the younger ones too; and he takes the whole picture for an emblem of wicked men, cruel persecutors and bloodthirsty tyrants who fill their palaces and kingdoms with murder and rapine.

The raven closes the chapter, and the contrast with the lion is the point. Wesley states it directly: having mentioned the noblest of the brute creatures God now mentions one of the most contemptible, to show the care of his providence over all, great and small; the young are so soon forsaken by their dams that without more than ordinary provision they would starve, and he draws the inference the verse invites, that he who provides for the young ravens will not fail to provide for his own children. Gill says the same of a creature voracious, mean and useless, fed not by man but by God. Clarke thinks the bird was chosen for its appetite and its continual cry, which is the cry of hunger, and because it dares not frequent the dwellings of men, being reckoned a bird of ill omen and hated by all; he quotes a poet's paraphrase of the verse and the note attached to it, that the raven is named as the care of Providence because her clamorous and importunate voice seems always to be calling upon it, and that the ravens on the banks of the Nile, being noisier than the rest of the species, are probably the ones meant. Ellicott corrects the grammar of the last clause, which is not a separate statement but dependent on what precedes, so that the wandering for lack of meat belongs with the crying.
